checkedAgainstDistrictMaterials: The NCCVT Health Curriculum Overview (Family Life and Sexuality, lessons 1 to 3) and the K-12 Health Education Concepts document (Reg. 551) were read. They set the framing: HIV prevention that stresses the benefits of abstinence; barrier, hormonal, and sterilization methods of contraception; consent and respecting personal boundaries. They contain no medical statistics.

claims.claim: Choosing no sexual activity removes the risk of sexual STI transmission and of pregnancy. A few infections (for example HIV and hepatitis B) can also spread in non-sexual ways, such as through shared needles.
claims.basis: Build brief section 2 (prompt-supplied) and district overview, lesson 3.
claims.check: CDC STI prevention page; HIV.gov how HIV spreads

claims.claim: Condoms used correctly and consistently greatly reduce, but do not eliminate, the risk of STIs (including HIV) and pregnancy.
claims.check: CDC condom effectiveness page; ACOG patient education on contraception

claims.claim: Many STIs have no symptoms, and testing is the only way to know whether a person has one.
claims.check: CDC STI basic information; MedlinePlus STIs

claims.claim: Bacterial STIs (chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis) are generally curable with antibiotics; viral STIs (HIV, herpes) are generally treatable or manageable, not curable; many HPV infections clear on their own; the HPV vaccine prevents infection with the types that cause most HPV cancers.
claims.check: CDC STI treatment guidelines; CDC HPV vaccination page

claims.claim: HIV is not spread by hugging, sharing utensils, toilet seats, saliva, sweat, or insect bites. It spreads through blood, semen, pre-seminal fluid, rectal and vaginal fluids, and breast milk, via sex without protection, sharing needles or syringes, and from parent to baby during pregnancy, birth, or breastfeeding.
A person living with HIV who takes treatment as prescribed and keeps an undetectable viral load does not sexually transmit HIV (undetectable = untransmittable).
claims.check: CDC HIV treatment as prevention page; HIV.gov U=U

claims.claim: Consent is freely given, informed, specific, ongoing, and can be withdrawn at any time; it cannot be given under pressure, threat, or incapacitation.
claims.basis: Build brief section 2 and Reg. 551 (consent and respecting personal boundaries).
claims.check: State or local health department sexual-violence-prevention page; CDC sexual violence prevention

claims.claim: Confidentiality rules for minors vary by state and by service; no service should be described as guaranteed confidential.
claims.check: Delaware Division of Public Health / state minor-consent guidance; AAP policy statement on adolescent confidentiality

claims.claim: Puberty timing varies widely among healthy people; hormones start puberty; acne is linked to hormones and oil production rather than to poor washing; shaving does not make hair grow back thicker or darker.
claims.basis: General health-education knowledge; not in the district overview.
claims.check: MedlinePlus puberty and acne pages; AAP HealthyChildren.org

claims.claim: Reproductive structures and their functions (ovary, fallopian tube, uterus, cervix, vagina, testis, epididymis, vas deferens, prostate gland, urethra); ovulation, fertilization in the fallopian tube, implantation, embryo, fetus, birth.
claims.basis: District overview, lesson 1 (structures, functions, ovulation, stages of pregnancy).
claims.check: MedlinePlus anatomy pages; ACOG pregnancy development page

claims.claim: Contraception falls into barrier, hormonal, and sterilization groups; hormonal methods and sterilization do not protect against STIs; condoms also reduce STI risk.
claims.check: CDC contraception page; ACOG contraception FAQs

claims.claim: Source credibility cues: named qualified authors, linked sources, recent date, no sales pitch, health agency or medical center publisher.
claims.basis: General media-literacy practice; course standard 3 (access information).
claims.check: School media specialist or a health-literacy guide from a public health agency

claims.claim: The STOP decision model: State the decision, Think of options, Observe consequences, Pick a responsible health-enhancing choice and explain why.
